screens.title: App Deployment for Android (Native & React Native)
screens.narratorSegment: Deployment is the final step that moves your app from a development environment into the hands of real users. In this lesson you will learn why signing and packaging matter, how the Google Play Console organizes releases, and the different build paths for native Android and React Native projects. We will make the abstract concrete: you will see how a release keystore protects your app’s identity and why the Android App Bundle leads to smaller user downloads. For React Native, you will learn how Expo’s managed workflow uses cloud builds and how a bare workflow maps back to the native toolchain. A common pitfall is treating the build artifact like an afterthought — losing a keystore or forgetting to increment versionCode can block updates. Throughout this module we emphasize reproducible steps, secure storage of credentials, and store-ready assets like icons and splash screens. By the end, you will understand the release pipeline end-to-end and be able to produce a signed AAB ready for Play Console upload. As you watch, think about what part of your current project needs a checklist for a smooth release.

App Deployment for Android

Prepare, sign, and publish Android apps with best practices for native and React Native workflows.

Terminal demo
Duration: ~20 min walkthrough
Why this matters

Signed bundles guarantee update authenticity and smaller downloads when distributed as AAB. Stores require proper assets and metadata to list your app.

Who benefits

Developers releasing production apps, team leads reviewing release pipelines, and learners preparing capstone apps for publication.

In this lesson

Build Artifacts

Visual overview

source code, android/app
Signing
keystore → signed AAB
Play Console
upload, tracks, listing
Explore Key Topics

AABs are preferred for optimized downloads; Play does final APK signing and delivery.
Expo Builds

screens.title: Why app signing and keystores matter
screens.narratorSegment: App signing is the cryptographic process that proves your app and its updates come from you. A keystore holds the private key that is used to sign release builds; Play Store uses this signature chain to accept future updates. If you lose the keystore or its passwords, you cannot publish updates under the same package name, which effectively prevents your existing users from receiving new versions. Signing is not about encryption of app contents; it's about identity and integrity. A concrete example: when you create a keystore and generate a signed Android App Bundle, the Play Console verifies the signature and records the signer. Later, when you upload an update, the Play Console checks that the update is signed with the same key. A common misconception is that a debug key will suffice for production — it will not. Debug keys are ephemeral and widely shared in tooling, so production releases must use a private, securely stored keystore. Key practices include storing the keystore outside the project repository, backing it up, and recording credentials in a secure secrets manager. What steps will you add to your project checklist to protect your upload key?

keyIdea.title: Signing Principle
keyIdea.text: Signing ties app updates to a single trusted identity. Protect the keystore and passwords to preserve update capability.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Signing & Keystore
Definition

What signing does

Signing assigns an unforgeable identity to your app and ensures the Play Console can verify the origin of future updates.

  • • Digital signature proves authenticity and integrity of a release artifact.
  • • Keystore contains the private key used to create signatures; protect it carefully.
  • • Play Console accepts updates only if they are signed with the same key recorded for that package name.
Common misconception

Using a debug key or committing a keystore to version control is unsafe and will break future updates.

Example & Commands
Generate a keystore with Java keytool as an example command. This creates a private key you will use to sign releases.
keytool -genkeypair -v -storepass <store_password> -keystore my-upload-key.keystore -alias my-key-alias -keypass <key_password> -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
Pro tip

Back up your keystore to a secure location outside the project directory and record passwords in a secure secrets manager.

Key takeaway

Keystores protect app identity. Losing them prevents updates — treat them like production credentials.

screens.title: Generate a signed AAB using Android Studio
screens.narratorSegment: Generating a signed Android App Bundle in Android Studio is a repeatable process you should master. Begin by ensuring versionCode and versionName are correct in your module's build. gradle. Then use Build → Generate Signed Bundle / APK, choose Android App Bundle, and either select an existing keystore or create a new one. If creating a new keystore, pick a secure path outside the project, choose a strong store and key password, and remember the alias. Select the release build variant and create the bundle. Android Studio will compile, sign, and place the generated. aab in your project’s output directory and present a Locate link. A concrete example: create a keystore at a secure path, set store password and alias, then choose release; the IDE performs tasks you can also script. Common errors include forgetting to select the release variant or not incrementing versionCode before upload. After generating the AAB, test it on devices if possible, and then upload to Play Console's internal or open testing track before production. What will you verify in your next local AAB build? Generate a signed AAB using Android Studio means use android studio's generate signed bundle flow to produce a signed aab, and always verify build variant, keystore, and versioning before building.. In practical terms, step-by-step: build → keystore → release variant → locate artifact. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Generate Signed AAB
Process

Steps to create a signed AAB

  1. 1
    Update versionCode and versionName in app/build.gradle.
  2. 2
    In Android Studio choose Build → Generate Signed Bundle / APK and pick Android App Bundle.
  3. 3
    Select or create a keystore; choose a secure path and strong passwords.
  4. 4
    Choose the release build variant and click Create. Locate the produced .aab via the IDE link.
Quick checklist

versionCode bumped, keystore path secured, release variant selected, artifact located and backed up.

Command callout
While Android Studio provides the GUI, you may also script gradle tasks. Example gradle commands illustrate building the bundle locally.
./gradlew bundleRelease
# This will produce an unsigned or signed AAB depending on your signing configuration in build.gradle or Gradle properties
Example

If you create a new keystore via the Android Studio dialog, record its path and passwords. Then run the bundle build and confirm a locate link appears in the IDE notifications.

Key Takeaway

Android Studio streamlines signing. Verify versioning and keystore before building to avoid blocked Play Console uploads.

screens.title: Google Play Console: create listing and release artifacts
screens.narratorSegment: The Google Play Console is where your signed AAB becomes publicly available. The process begins with registering a developer account and creating a new application record where you choose name and default language. The Store Listing section is critical: you must provide app name, short and full descriptions, a high-resolution icon, screenshots, and optional promo media. These assets heavily influence conversion, so invest in clear screenshots and concise descriptions. Next, the App Releases section lets you upload the signed AAB to a track — internal, closed, open, or production — each serving different testing and distribution goals. For initial verification use an internal or open testing track to roll out to small groups. You must also complete content rating and pricing & distribution sections and provide an app content declaration including privacy policy. A frequent mistake is failing to increment versionCode prior to uploading a new release or leaving required fields blank, which prevents publishing. As a final step, use internal testing or a staged rollout to validate the release before moving to production. Which track will you choose for your first published build?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Play Console
Definition

What the Play Console manages

Store listing
App name, short & full descriptions, screenshots, icon, feature graphic.
App releases
Upload signed AAB to tracks: internal, closed, open, or production.
App content
Privacy policy, target audience, content rating, ads declaration.
Concrete steps
  1. 1. Create app in Play Console and set default language.
  2. 2. Fill Store Listing with high-quality screenshots and a descriptive summary.
  3. 3. Upload signed AAB under App Releases and pick a track for rollout.
  4. 4. Complete Content Rating and Pricing & Distribution sections.
Example

For your first public test, upload the AAB to an internal testing track and invite testers. After verification, promote the release to production or use staged rollout.

Key Takeaway

Play Console enforces metadata and policy checks. Use testing tracks first and ensure versionCode increments for updates.

screens.title: React Native deployment: Expo managed vs bare workflow
screens.narratorSegment: React Native apps can be released using different workflows, and the tooling you use affects how you build and sign your Android artifact. In the Expo managed workflow, Expo Application Services can build a signed AAB for you on cloud servers, and Expo can optionally manage your keystore so you don’t handle signing locally. The primary command for a production build is eas build --platform android --profile production, which queues a cloud build and returns a downloadable AAB. This simplifies signing but requires trust in Expo’s service or careful keystore configuration if you supply your own. In a bare React Native workflow — or an ejected Expo app — you work with the android directory and Android Studio as with a native project: generate a keystore, configure build. gradle, and build a signed AAB locally. A common misconception is that Expo always eliminates the need to understand native signing; even with managed builds you must configure package names, versionCode, and app. json correctly. A practical suggestion: use Expo for faster managed builds during early releases, and migrate to bare workflow when you need native modules or tighter control over signing. Which workflow aligns with your project's native requirements?

keyIdea.title: Workflow Choice
keyIdea.text: Expo managed simplifies cloud builds and optional keystore management; bare workflow offers full native control and mirrors native Android steps.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Expo vs Bare
Expo Managed Workflow

Cloud builds and optional keystore management

Expo handles much of the native build complexity. Configure app.json with package name, version, icon, and splash; then run EAS to build.
eas build --platform android --profile production
  • • Expo can manage your keystore or accept one you provide.
  • • Produces a signed AAB you download and upload to Play Console.
  • • Faster iteration for JS-driven apps without native dependencies.
Bare / Ejected Workflow

Full control via Android Studio and Gradle

You work with the android directory, generate a keystore, configure build.gradle signingConfigs, and build a signed AAB locally or in CI.
# Typical keystore generation
keytool -genkeypair -v -storepass <store_password> -keystore my-upload-key.keystore -alias my-key-alias -keypass <key_password> -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
  • • Mirrors native Android signing and build steps.
  • • Required when using native modules or custom native code.
  • • You must manage keystore files and Gradle properties securely.
When to use Expo

When you prefer cloud builds and your app relies mostly on JS and supported APIs.

When to go bare

When you need native modules, full Gradle control, or custom signing workflows.

Common pitfall

Assuming Expo removes the need to understand versionCode, package name, and signing—these still matter.

screens.title: Pre-deployment checklist: versioning, icons, privacy, and testing
screens.narratorSegment: A short checklist before you upload an AAB will save hours of rework. Start with versioning: increment versionCode for every release and update versionName to reflect user-visible changes. Next, verify all required assets — high-resolution app icon, feature graphic, and screenshots for relevant device sizes — because poor assets reduce discoverability or trigger rejection. Ensure your privacy policy is written and reachable via a public URL and that you have completed all Play Console app content questions, including advertising and target audience declarations. Test the release build on multiple devices and A P I levels; release builds use optimizations like R8 and may behave differently from debug builds. Also, confirm your build includes production configuration (A P I keys, endpoints, and ProGuard/R8 rules) and that sensitive credentials are not bundled in plain text. Common mistakes include committing keystore files, forgetting to bump versionCode, and leaving the store listing incomplete. Before upload, run through the checklist and use an internal testing track for a final verification step. Which two items on this checklist will you add as mandatory before every upload?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Pre-deployment Checklist
Definition

Checklist for a successful release

Versioning

Bump versionCode and update versionName in build files. Play Console requires a higher versionCode for updates.

Assets

Provide high-res icon, screenshots, and feature graphic. Poor visuals hurt discovery and may delay approval.

Privacy & Declarations

Publish a privacy policy URL and complete content/ad declarations in the Play Console.

Testing

Install and run release builds on multiple devices and use testing tracks before production rollout.

Common mistakes
  • • Forgetting to increase versionCode before uploading a new release.
  • • Committing keystore files or passwords to version control.
  • • Leaving required Play Console fields blank, blocking publishing.
Key Takeaway

A short pre-upload checklist prevents common rejections. Test release builds and protect signing credentials before uploading.

screens.title: Manage signing credentials securely (teams & CI)
screens.narratorSegment: You will almost always work as part of a team or use continuous integration to build release artifacts. That makes secure key management essential. Treat your keystore and its passwords like any other production secret: keep them out of source control, limit who can access them, and back them up offline. A practical pattern is to store the keystore file in a secure artifact store or an encrypted secrets manager, and then expose only short-lived access to CI agents. For local development, place the keystore outside your project folder and reference it by an environment variable or a developer-only configuration file that is gitignored. Remember the cost of loss: if you lose the keystore and passwords, you cannot publish updates to the same app identifier. One common misconception is that keeping the keystore in a private repository is sufficient; it is not. Repositories can be leaked or cloned. Use OS-level file permissions, vault services, or your CI provider's secret storage to rotate and revoke access when someone leaves the team. As a short checklist: back up the keystore in two secure locations, never commit passwords, prefer CI secret stores for production builds, and document the recovery procedure. Reflect: when was the last time your project reviewed who has signing access?

keyIdea.text: Treat keystores as irreversible secrets: back them up, use CI secret stores, and never commit credentials to source control.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Manage signing credentials securely
Core Concept

Keystore lifecycle

Define ownership, backup policy, and access controls for your application's signing keystore.

Mnemonic: Think of the keystore as a vault key — store it offline and give access sparingly.
Practical patterns
  • Place keystore outside project directory and reference it with env vars.
  • Use CI secret management to inject keystore and passwords only at build time.
  • Keep encrypted backups in two different secure locations.
  • Log and audit who builds and who retrieves signing artifacts.
Architecture

Team + CI signing flow

Developer
Local devs use a test keystore and env variables for builds.
CI / Build Server
Inject keystore from secure store at build time only.
Backup Vault
Encrypted, offline backups to recover lost keys.
Key Takeaway

Protect and back up signing keys, keep them out of version control, and automate secure injection during CI builds.

screens.title: Gradle signingConfigs and secure properties
screens.narratorSegment: When you control the Android project you must teach the build system where to find signing credentials without embedding them in source. The usual approach is to define a signingConfigs. release block in android/app/build. gradle that references properties populated from environment variables or a local gradle. properties file. Doing this keeps passwords out of version control yet accessible to the build. A clear pitfall is storing the keystore file inside the repository; instead place it in a developer-only folder or provide it from CI. When running locally, populate ~/. gradle/gradle. properties or export environment variables. In CI, use the provider's secret store so the build agent can set those variables at build time. If you need to debug signing, temporarily echo the resolved file path on a safe, non-production machine rather than printing secrets to logs. keyIdea.title: Reference secrets, don't commit them

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Gradle signingConfigs
Code Walkthrough

Reference properties in signingConfigs

Do not commit passwords. Use env vars or ~/.gradle/gradle.properties instead.

Example build.gradle snippet
<!-- android/app/build.gradle (excerpt) -->
android {
  signingConfigs {
    release {
      if (project.hasProperty('MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE')) {
        storeFile file(MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_FILE)
        storePassword MYAPP_UPLOAD_STORE_PASSWORD
        keyAlias MYAPP_UPLOAD_KEY_ALIAS
        keyPassword MYAPP_UPLOAD_KEY_PASSWORD
      }
    }
  }
  buildTypes {
    release {
      signingConfig signingConfigs.release
      minifyEnabled enableProguardInReleaseBuilds
      proguardFiles getDefaultProguardFile("proguard-android.txt"), "proguard-rules.pro"
    }
  }
}
Place the actual secrets in ~/.gradle/gradle.properties or set corresponding environment variables in CI.
Secure storage options
  • Local developer: store secrets in ~/.gradle/gradle.properties (gitignored).
  • CI: use the provider's secret store and inject at build time.
  • Avoid printing passwords in build logs; log only paths or non-sensitive status messages.
Key Takeaway

Make Gradle read secrets from properties or env vars so the repository never contains signing credentials.

screens.title: Generate a keystore with keytool
screens.narratorSegment: Generating a keystore is a concrete step you will take before your first production release. The Java keytool utility is the standard tool for this. The important flags are the keystore path, the store and key passwords, an alias that identifies which key to use, the key algorithm and key size, and the validity period. In practice, choose a strong password, a clear alias like uploadkey, and a long validity. When you run the keytool command, store the generated keystore outside your project directory and immediately back it up to an encrypted vault. A common misconception is that you can later recreate the same keystore; you cannot regenerate the exact private key from the same parameters. Keep the alias and passwords documented in a secure team vault. For debugging, avoid sharing the keystore file; instead share a test keystore for collaborators. The visual example shows the canonical keytool command you will use. After creating the keystore, configure the Android project to reference it and verify you can build a signed bundle. Finally, consider storing the upload key separately from CI-only keys if you need to rotate credentials later.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Generate keystore
Process

Create a keystore with keytool

Run the keytool command, back up the file, and keep passwords secure.

Canonical keytool command
keytool -genkeypair -v -storepass <your_store_password> -keystore my-upload-key.keystore -alias my-key-alias -keypass <your_key_password> -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000
Replace placeholders with strong passwords and store the resulting .keystore file securely.
Field notes
  • storepass / keypass: Protect these; do not print them in logs.
  • alias: Use a memorable name like uploadkey to simplify future updates.
  • validity: Choose a long period; many choose 10,000 days to avoid expiry issues.
Key Takeaway

Generate your keystore once, back it up securely, and never commit it to your project repo.

screens.title: ProGuard / R8: shrink, obfuscate, and test release builds
screens.narratorSegment: Release builds often differ from debug builds because of optimizations like code shrinking, obfuscation, and resource removal. Tools such as ProGuard and R8 reduce app size and make reverse engineering harder, but they can also remove code that looks unused to the optimizer or rename symbols libraries rely on. This can lead to bugs that only appear in release builds. To avoid surprises, adopt a release-testing workflow: build a local signed release AAB or APK, install it on multiple test devices and A P I levels, and exercise features that use reflection, native libraries, or dynamic loading. If you encounter a crash in release but not in debug, consult the mapping file generated during the build to map obfuscated class names back to readable names. Another practical debug step is to temporarily disable minification while diagnosing the issue, which narrows the search. Keep carefully curated proguard-rules. pro entries to preserve classes used by serialization, reflection, or external libraries, and treat those rules as part of your repository (they do not contain secrets). A common misconception is that enabling minify always increases risk; in reality, minify helps performance but requires testing. End with this question: which parts of your app rely on reflection or code generation and therefore need explicit keep rules?

keyIdea.text: Minification and obfuscation can introduce release-only bugs. Always build and test signed release artifacts before publishing.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › ProGuard & R8
Definition

What ProGuard and R8 do

They shrink unused code, rename symbols, and optimize resources to reduce APK/AAB size and harden the app.

Why this matters: smaller downloads, lower storage usage.
What to watch: reflection and libraries that depend on class names.
Release-test checklist
  1. Generate a signed release AAB and install it on real devices.
  2. Test features that use reflection, serialization, or dynamic loading.
  3. If crashes occur, build mapping files and consult them to decode stack traces.
  4. Temporarily disable minify to isolate the problematic rules, then add explicit keep rules.
Common mistake

Assuming debug testing is enough. Release builds must be validated because of optimizations like R8.

Key Takeaway

Always include signed release builds in test plans and keep proguard rules under source control.

screens.title: Testing tracks, staged rollouts, and localization
screens.narratorSegment: Publishing is as much about distribution strategy as a clean binary. Google Play offers multiple tracks—internal, closed, open testing, and production—that let you stage releases to progressively larger audiences. Start with an internal or closed test to verify the signed AAB on representative devices. A staged rollout to a small percentage helps you detect critical issues before affecting all users. Localization is another lever: translate your store listing and app strings for key markets to improve discoverability and adoption. Make sure localized screenshots and short descriptions are accurate for each locale you target. A frequent mistake is pushing a global release without validating translations or testing region-specific behaviors. Also remember content rating and privacy declarations must match what your localized builds do. Monitor Play Console reports during rollouts to watch crash rates and active users. If a regression appears, use the internal track to push a hotfix build quickly. Ask yourself: which countries or languages deserve a cautious first rollout, and what telemetry will you watch to stop a bad release fast? Testing tracks, staged rollouts, and localization means use testing tracks and staged rollouts to catch issues early and localize store assets to reach and convert users in target markets.. In practical terms, use play console tracks and localization to reduce risk and reach more users. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Rollouts & Localization
Comparison

Testing tracks at a glance

Internal testing: fastest, for a handful of testers.
Closed testing: curated groups for staged QA.
Open testing: public beta before production.
Production: staged rollout percentages for cautious delivery.
Staged rollout example
  1. Upload signed AAB to internal track for smoke tests.
  2. Move to closed testing for a broader QA group.
  3. Start a 5% staged rollout in production and monitor crash rate.
  4. Increase rollout if metrics are healthy, or halt and fix if not.
Localization tips
  • Translate store listing and screenshots for target locales.
  • Test locale-specific behavior on devices configured for that language.
  • Align privacy policy and content declarations across locales.
Key Takeaway

Use test tracks and staged rollouts to protect users, and localize store assets for better reach.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's recap the most important deployment concepts you will use repeatedly. First, app signing and keystores are your identity: keep the keystore and its passwords secure, back them up, and use CI secret stores to avoid committing them. Second, the Android App Bundle is the preferred format to publish on Google Play because it enables optimized, smaller downloads. Third, manage versioning carefully—increment versionCode for every Play Store update—and ensure your build. gradle references secure properties or environment variables. Fourth, test signed release builds early because tools like ProGuard and R8 can alter runtime behavior; keep mapping files and proguard rules under source control. Finally, use Play Console testing tracks and staged rollouts to verify releases before reaching all users, and localize store assets to improve discoverability. These are the practical rules that minimize release risk and keep your app updateable for the long term.

Backup keystore
Store at least two encrypted backups outside the project and document recovery steps.

Play Console rejects updates without a higher versionCode than your previous release.

Install a signed AAB or APK on devices and verify functionality under release optimizations.

A careful pre-publish checklist and staged rollout are your best defenses against release-time surprises. Verify keys, builds, and listings before upload.

fullNarratorScript:
Deployment is the final step that moves your app from a development environment into the hands of real users. In this lesson you will learn why signing and packaging matter, how the Google Play Console organizes releases, and the different build paths for native Android and React Native projects. We will make the abstract concrete: you will see how a release keystore protects your app’s identity and why the Android App Bundle leads to smaller user downloads. For React Native, you will learn how Expo’s managed workflow uses cloud builds and how a bare workflow maps back to the native toolchain. A common pitfall is treating the build artifact like an afterthought — losing a keystore or forgetting to increment versionCode can block updates. Throughout this module we emphasize reproducible steps, secure storage of credentials, and store-ready assets like icons and splash screens. By the end, you will understand the release pipeline end-to-end and be able to produce a signed AAB ready for Play Console upload. As you watch, think about what part of your current project needs a checklist for a smooth release.

These learning objectives map directly to the practical steps you will take while preparing an app for release. First, you will learn the concrete steps to prepare a native Android app for release, including signing and packaging. Second, you will generate a signed APK or Android App Bundle using Android Studio, making choices such as release build variant and keystore configuration. Third, you will navigate the Google Play Console: creating an app record, filling the store listing, choosing a release track, and uploading artifacts. Finally, you will prepare a React Native application for release, understanding the differences between Expo managed builds and bare or ejected workflows. Each objective includes a measurable action: create or locate a keystore, produce a signed AAB, complete required Play Console forms, and run a cloud or local build. These are practical skills you will apply while completing the hands-on activity. As you work, confirm you can both create an artifact and explain why each pre-deployment check—like versionCode increments and icon sizes—matters for a successful release.

This second objectives slide drills into the checks that commonly cause release delays and how to prevent them. You will learn to version correctly by incrementing versionCode and aligning versionName to your release strategy. You will confirm app icons and splash screens are provided at high resolution for multiple densities, avoiding rejected store listings for poor assets. You will verify privacy policy and content declarations required by the Play Console and test release builds on devices because release builds enable optimizations that can hide debug-only behavior. Lastly, you will practice safe keystore handling: where to store it, how to back it up, and why losing it prevents updates. These measurable outcomes will help you construct a pre-release checklist and avoid common mistakes such as missing assets, stale version codes, or policies left incomplete. By the end, you should be able to run through a checklist that ensures an AAB can be uploaded and accepted by Play Console.

App signing is the cryptographic process that proves your app and its updates come from you. A keystore holds the private key that is used to sign release builds; Play Store uses this signature chain to accept future updates. If you lose the keystore or its passwords, you cannot publish updates under the same package name, which effectively prevents your existing users from receiving new versions. Signing is not about encryption of app contents; it's about identity and integrity. A concrete example: when you create a keystore and generate a signed Android App Bundle, the Play Console verifies the signature and records the signer. Later, when you upload an update, the Play Console checks that the update is signed with the same key. A common misconception is that a debug key will suffice for production — it will not. Debug keys are ephemeral and widely shared in tooling, so production releases must use a private, securely stored keystore. Key practices include storing the keystore outside the project repository, backing it up, and recording credentials in a secure secrets manager. What steps will you add to your project checklist to protect your upload key?

Generating a signed Android App Bundle in Android Studio is a repeatable process you should master. Begin by ensuring versionCode and versionName are correct in your module's build. gradle. Then use Build → Generate Signed Bundle / APK, choose Android App Bundle, and either select an existing keystore or create a new one. If creating a new keystore, pick a secure path outside the project, choose a strong store and key password, and remember the alias. Select the release build variant and create the bundle. Android Studio will compile, sign, and place the generated. aab in your project’s output directory and present a Locate link. A concrete example: create a keystore at a secure path, set store password and alias, then choose release; the IDE performs tasks you can also script. Common errors include forgetting to select the release variant or not incrementing versionCode before upload. After generating the AAB, test it on devices if possible, and then upload to Play Console's internal or open testing track before production. What will you verify in your next local AAB build? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Google Play Console is where your signed AAB becomes publicly available. The process begins with registering a developer account and creating a new application record where you choose name and default language. The Store Listing section is critical: you must provide app name, short and full descriptions, a high-resolution icon, screenshots, and optional promo media. These assets heavily influence conversion, so invest in clear screenshots and concise descriptions. Next, the App Releases section lets you upload the signed AAB to a track — internal, closed, open, or production — each serving different testing and distribution goals. For initial verification use an internal or open testing track to roll out to small groups. You must also complete content rating and pricing & distribution sections and provide an app content declaration including privacy policy. React Native apps can be released using different workflows, and the tooling you use affects how you build and sign your Android artifact. Which workflow aligns with your project's native requirements?

Common mistakes include committing keystore files, forgetting to bump versionCode, and leaving the store listing incomplete. Before upload, run through the checklist and use an internal testing track for a final verification step. Which two items on this checklist will you add as mandatory before every upload?
